alignment.note: ἀλλά / ܐܠܐ / Sed — adversative conjunction; the parenthetical transliteration (all᾽) is editorial.

Greek ὑπάγετε and Latin ite are present imperatives ('go!'), whereas the Syriac ܙܠܝܢ is a participial/predicative form functioning as an imperative; the verbal aspect is rendered idiomatically rather than morphologically matched.

The Greek dative article τοῖς governing μαθηταῖς has no separate token in Syriac (carried by the prefix ܠ- on ܠܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ) or in Latin (which renders an articleless dative discipulis); a routine structural difference rather than a textual variant.
μαθηταῖς αὐτοῦ / ܠܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ / discipulis ejus — 'to his disciples'; Syriac fuses preposition, noun, and possessive suffix into a single word.
καί / ܘ- / et — coordinating conjunction; in Syriac the conjunction is prefixed to the following noun.

Greek and Latin transliterate the Greek name Πέτρῳ / Petro, whereas the Peshitta preserves the underlying Aramaic ܟܐܦܐ (Kepha, 'rock'), the original Semitic form that Πέτρος itself translates (cf. John 1:42); this is a lexical, not merely orthographic, witness.

Greek ὅτι and Latin quia introduce indirect/direct discourse ('that'); the Syriac renders this with ܕܗܐ, combining the relative/complementiser ܕ- with the presentative particle ܗܐ ('behold'), adding a deictic emphasis absent from the Greek and Latin.
ὑμᾶς / ܠܟܘܢ / vos — second person plural object.
εἰς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν / ܠܓܠܝܠܐ / in Galilæam — 'into Galilee'; the Greek punctuation (·) and the Latin colon are handled with the geographic clause.
αὐτὸν ὄψεσθε / ܬܚܙܘܢܝܗܝ / eum videbitis — 'you will see him'; Syriac compresses verb and pronominal object into a single suffixed form.
καθὼς / ܐܝܟܢܐ / sicut — comparative particle 'just as'.
εἶπεν / ܕܐܡܪ / dixit — 'he said'; Syriac prefixes the relative ܕ- to the verb.
ὑμῖν / ܠܟܘܢ / vobis — second person plural dative 'to you'.
